name: Ubaid culture
title: The story of the Ubaid culture

text: About 8,500 years ago, people began to settle on the flat river lands of southern Iraq.
Archaeologists call their way of life the Ubaid culture, after a place called Tell al-Ubaid.
src: The Ubaid period left the earliest known settlements on the southern Mesopotamian plain / c. 6500 BCE: The Ubaid period begins in southern Mesopotamia / Mesopotamia (Iraq)
The Ubaid period takes its name from Tell al-ʿUbaid in southern Iraq

text: They lived in big villages of mud-brick houses and built the first temples in Mesopotamia.
Their pots were painted with black patterns on a pale yellow-brown background.
src: large unwalled villages, multi-roomed rectangular mud-brick houses and the first temples of public architecture in Mesopotamia

text: Farmers grew barley, wheat, lentils and flax, and kept sheep, goats, cattle and pigs.
On the coast, people fished and even caught tuna.
src: farmers grew barley, wheat, lentil, ervil and flax / domesticated sheep, goats, cattle and pigs
On the Gulf coast people fished in shallow waters and even caught tuna.

text: A clay disc from Kuwait shows a boat with two masts, the oldest sign of sails anywhere.
Their pots spread along the Persian Gulf, perhaps traded for dates, shell jewellery or fish.
src: A clay disc from the site of H3 in Kuwait shows a two-masted boat, the oldest evidence for the use of masts and sails.
Along the Persian Gulf, Ubaid pottery appeared / Local imitations suggest that the pottery itself was traded, perhaps for dates, pearl and shell jewellery, animals or fish

text: Their ideas and styles spread north as far as Turkey, mostly in peace rather than by war.
They buried their dead with beads, necklaces and pots, perhaps holding food.
src: Ubaid pottery and customs spread from south-eastern Turkey to the Persian Gulf, according to Gil Stein and Rana Özbal largely through the peaceful spread of ideas rather than conquest
They were given beads, necklaces and headdresses, pots presumably holding food

text: About 5,800 years ago, the Ubaid age gave way to the Uruk period, when the first real cities grew.
Their temples, painted pots and graves, dug up by archaeologists, still tell their story.
src: c. 3800 BCE: The Ubaid period gives way to the Uruk period in the south / there were still no real cities: those came in the Uruk period that followed
Excavations from 1919 on (Tell al-ʿUbaid, Eridu, Ur, the Hamrin sites, ʿOueili, Tell Zeidan, Gulf coast sites), pottery sequences, burials
